Moral Foundations Theory is a framework that separates human morality into the following categories:

  - Care/Harm: related to our long evolution as mammals with attachment systems
    and an ability to feel (and dislike) the pain of others. It underlies the
    virtues of kindness, gentleness, and nurturance.

  - Loyalty/Betrayal: related to our long history as tribal creatures able to
    form shifting coalitions. It is active anytime people feel that it is "one
    for all and all for one." It underlies the virtues of patriotism and
    self-sacrifice for the group.

  - Authority/Subversion: shaped by our long primate history of hierarchical
    social interactions. It underlies virtues of leadership and followership,
    including deference to prestigious authority figures and respect for
    traditions.

  - Sanctity/Purity: shaped by the psychology of disgust and contamination. It
    underlies notions of striving to live in an elevated, less carnal, more
    noble, and more "natural" way (often present in religious narratives). This
    foundation underlies the widespread idea that the body is a temple that can
    be desecrated by immoral activities and contaminants (an idea not unique to
    religious traditions). It underlies the virtues of self-discipline,
    self-improvement, naturalness, and spirituality.

  - Equality: related to our intuitions about equal treatment and equal outcome
    for individuals.

  - Proportionality: related to our intuitions about individuals getting
    rewarded in proportion to their merit or contribution.

Every category has a bidirectional nature. For example:

One person's sensitivity to the Care/Harm foundation may lead them to support high levels of immigration from poorer nations, to reduce the suffering of those who migrate. Whereas another person's sensitivity to the very same foundation may lead them to oppose those levels, because they believe it could lead to people they care about being harmed.

# Summary of Political Manifesto

This document presents a comprehensive policy platform centered on addressing climate change and environmental concerns, proposing a "Green New Deal" framework with investment exceeding £100 billion annually across multiple sectors.

## Environmental and Energy Policies

The manifesto prioritizes transitioning to renewable energy, aiming for net-zero carbon emissions by 2030. Key proposals include replacing fossil fuels with wind, solar, tidal, and other renewable sources, with wind potentially providing 70% of electricity. The document advocates banning fracking, prohibiting new nuclear power stations, removing fossil fuel subsidies, and implementing a Carbon Tax on imports and domestic extraction.

## Housing and Buildings

The plan proposes creating 100,000 new council homes annually built to high energy-efficiency standards, improving insulation for all homes requiring it, and delivering major heating upgrades to one million homes yearly. All new buildings would meet strict energy performance requirements.

## Transport

Transportation reforms include expanding rail capacity, electrifying railway lines, creating new cycleways and footpaths, reducing public transport costs, and ending sales of new petrol and diesel vehicles by 2030. The document opposes new runway construction and proposes cancelling a high-speed rail project.

## Economic and Social Reforms

A Universal Basic Income of £89 weekly for adults and £178 for pensioners would replace most income-related benefits. The manifesto proposes increasing the minimum wage to £12, providing 35 hours of free childcare, and implementing a maximum wage ratio of 10:1 within organizations.

## Democratic Reforms

Electoral reforms include replacing first-past-the-post voting with proportional representation, lowering voting age to 16, creating an elected upper legislative chamber, and devolving more power to local authorities.

## Taxation

Revenue proposals include increasing corporation tax to 24%, simplifying income taxes by merging multiple tax categories, implementing a Land Value Tax replacing council tax and business rates, and cracking down on tax avoidance.

## Healthcare and Education

NHS funding would increase by £6 billion annually, with privatization rolled back. Education funding would rise by £4 billion, tuition fees would be abolished, and existing student debt from higher fee regimes would be written off.

## International Policy

The document advocates remaining in the European Union, increasing foreign aid to 1% of gross national income, prioritizing climate emergency in international spending, and reforming trade agreements to maintain environmental standards.

## Agriculture and Land Use

Agricultural reforms include transitioning to sustainable farming practices, planting 700 million trees, reducing pesticide use by 50%, and supporting local food systems. The manifesto proposes ending intensive livestock farming and introducing taxes on meat and dairy products.

## Drug Policy

The document advocates repealing existing drug prohibition laws, legalizing and regulating drug access, treating addiction as a health issue, and pardoning those convicted of possession offenses.

# Summary of 2019 UK General Election Manifesto

This manifesto outlines policy commitments across several key areas, focusing on leaving the European Union and subsequent domestic priorities.

## Brexit
The central pledge is completing EU withdrawal by January, implementing a negotiated agreement that removes the UK from EU customs arrangements and single market rules. This would enable independent trade policy, border controls, and regulatory autonomy. The manifesto emphasises this as essential before other priorities can be addressed.

## Healthcare
Major NHS commitments include £34 billion additional annual funding, recruitment of 50,000 nurses and 6,000 doctors, 50 million extra GP appointments annually, and construction of 40 new hospitals. Mental health services would receive equal priority to physical health. A visa scheme would fast-track qualified overseas health workers. Social care would receive £1 billion annually, with cross-party work sought on long-term reform, guaranteeing nobody would need to sell their home for care costs.

## Education and Skills
Schools would receive £14 billion over three years, with minimum funding of £5,000 per secondary pupil and £4,000 per primary pupil. Teacher starting salaries would rise to £30,000. A £3 billion National Skills Fund would support adult retraining, alongside upgraded further education colleges and apprenticeship expansion.

## Public Safety
Twenty thousand additional police officers would be recruited. Sentencing for serious crimes would be toughened, automatic early release ended for serious offenders, and knife crime addressed through new court orders. Victim support legislation and domestic abuse measures feature prominently.

## Immigration
An Australian-style points-based system would replace freedom of movement, prioritising skilled workers with job offers. Five-year residency requirements would apply before accessing certain benefits. Settlement scheme protections continue for existing EU residents.

## Economic Policy
Commitments include no increases to income tax, VAT, or National Insurance rates, plus raising the National Insurance threshold. The National Living Wage would increase to £10.50 hourly. Business rates would be reviewed and reduced for retail. Borrowing rules limit investment to 3% of GDP while avoiding day-to-day deficit spending.

## Infrastructure
Major transport investments include Northern Powerhouse Rail, Midlands Rail Hub, and nationwide gigabit broadband by 2025. Electric vehicle charging networks would expand. Town regeneration funds would support local improvements.

## Environment
Net zero emissions by 2050 remains the target. Offshore wind capacity would reach 40GW by 2030. Tree planting would increase to 75,000 acres annually. Plastic waste exports to non-OECD countries would be banned. A fracking moratorium continues.

## Housing
Targets include 300,000 homes annually by mid-2020s. Long-term fixed-rate mortgages would reduce deposit requirements. Local discount schemes would prioritise first-time buyers. "No fault" evictions would be abolished for renters.

## Defence and Foreign Policy
Defence spending would exceed 2% of GDP with annual increases. Nuclear deterrent maintenance continues. Trade agreements targeting 80% coverage within three years are planned, including with the USA, Australia, and New Zealand. The 0.7% development aid commitment remains.
